w: Started as a cooking-oil retailer in 1958 and only turned to dumplings in 1972; the Xinyi Road counter still hand-pleats xiaolongbao to eighteen folds and weighs each one to the gram. Every branch worldwide, from Shanghai to Seattle, measures itself against this original room.
s: The soup dumpling that built a global empire
why: Remains the reference standard as Din Tai Fung expands globally, with the flagship now a four-storey dine-in hall opened in 2020.

w: A former red-light backstreet turned open-air food walk: charcoal smoke, tanks of live seafood and rows of grilled stingray, chicken wings and hokkien mee spilling across the closed-off lane every night. Officially pedestrianised in 2023, it now runs car-free from six until three.
s: A red-light backstreet reborn as a food walk
why: Made a permanent car-free 'Food Walk' in 2023, cementing its status as KL's most concentrated night-eating strip.

w: Southeast Asia's largest Chinatown strip lights up after dusk with woks of pad see ew, charcoal seafood grills and eighty-year-old fishball-noodle stalls whose bouncing balls are still made from hand-pounded fresh fish. Neon signage, some over a century old, spells out the street's Chinese-Thai lineage.
s: Two centuries of neon, woks and fishball noodles
why: A perennial Michelin street-food pick, drawing renewed crowds as Bangkok's Chinatown becomes a heritage-tourism draw.

w: Founded by a cook said to have served the last Mughal court, tucked down a lane by Jama Masjid since 1913. The mutton burra, seekh kebabs and korma still come off charcoal in a kitchen barely changed in a century, plastic chairs packed under strings of bare bulbs at any hour.
s: Mughal court cooking down a lane since 1913
why: Still the reference point for Old Delhi's Mughlai cooking as the city's heritage food trails draw growing global attention.

w: A single narrow lane off Chandni Chowk where a Gwalior Brahmin family began frying stuffed parathas in the late 1800s; their descendants still run rival shops side by side, deep-frying potato, paneer, even rabri-stuffed parathas in ghee on tavas set right at the doorway.
s: One lane, a century of deep-fried stuffed parathas
why: A century-plus dynasty of side-by-side family shops that remains Old Delhi's most concentrated single-dish food lane.

w: Nicknamed Osaka's Kitchen, a 580-metre covered arcade of some 150 stalls dating to the Edo period, rebuilt after wartime bombing into the city's postwar food supply hub. Crab legs, sea urchin and skewered wagyu now go straight from tank or grill into visitors' hands as they walk.
s: Osaka's Kitchen, grilling since the Edo period
why: One of Japan's most-visited food markets, riding the postpandemic surge in inbound tourism to Kansai.

w: A dim sum room on South Maoming Road that became the first of its kind in China to win a Michelin star, in the 2025 Shanghai guide. Founder Chen Lina separates hairy crab into eight components by hand for a crab-roe xiaolongbao, folding meat, roe and paste into one skin per basket.
s: China's first Michelin-starred dim sum counter
why: Awarded Shanghai's first-ever Michelin star for a dim sum restaurant in the November 2024 guide reveal.

w: Chef Alvaro Clavijo forages forgotten Colombian ingredients, ants, wild tubers, Amazonian fish, for a tasting menu served in a bohemian Chapinero Alto townhouse. Since opening in 2017 it has climbed steadily through the region's rankings on the strength of native produce rarely seen on a plate.
s: Forgotten Colombian ingredients, reimagined
why: Named No.1 on Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2025, the first Colombian restaurant ever to top the list.

w: Chef Mitsuharu Tsumura, born in Lima to a Japanese immigrant family, trained in Osaka before opening this Nikkei tasting-menu counter in 2009, threading sushi technique through Peruvian ceviche, causa and Amazonian ingredients. A single tuna-and-tiger's-milk course anchors the whole menu.
s: Nikkei fusion from a Lima-born, Osaka-trained chef
why: Named the World's Best Restaurant for 2025 by the World's 50 Best awards, the first Peruvian restaurant to top the global list.

w: A husband-and-wife cobblestone-street kitchen in Pinheiros where chef Lucas Dante smokes, ferments and cures everything in house, from butter to sausage, sourced from small growers he name-checks on the menu. Sommelier Gabrielli Fleming pairs it all with an all-Brazilian wine list.
s: House-cured, house-smoked, all from small growers
why: A fresh 2025 entry on Latin America's 50 Best list, part of Sao Paulo's biggest showing yet on the regional ranking.

w: An open-fire kitchen under jungle canopy off the Boca Paila road, built by a former Noma Mexico researcher who cooks Yucatan ingredients almost entirely over live flame. Smoke, palm thatch and candlelight replace any written menu; dishes arrive as the fire and the day's catch dictate.
s: Open-fire jungle kitchen off the Boca Paila road
why: A fresh 2025 entry on the World's 50 Best extended list, the highest new name from Mexico's fast-rising Riviera Maya scene.

w: A cast-iron pavilion shipped from Glasgow and raised in 1872 over the ashes of the old colonial marketplace, its eight wrought-iron roofs still ribbing the hall like a railway shed. Fishmongers and marisco counters trade beneath them, feeding the seafood restaurants wedged among the stalls.
s: Glasgow ironwork over Santiago's seafood trade
why: A national monument that remains the anchor of Santiago's seafood culture, drawing chefs and tourists alike each morning.

w: Every evening as the Koutoubia minaret dims, some fifty numbered stalls fire up beneath the same square where storytellers and snake charmers have performed for centuries. Grilled lamb tangia, snails in cumin broth and merguez smoke rise together over what UNESCO lists as intangible heritage.
s: Fifty stalls firing up under a UNESCO-listed square
why: Still the definitive nightly street-food theatre of North Africa, drawing record tourist numbers to Marrakech's medina.

w: For two decades a stretch of Glover Court in Ikoyi has drawn Lagosians for smoky, chilli-crusted suya, beef, kidney, tozo and gizzard skewered and fanned over open coals by grillmen working late into the night. No seating to speak of, just a queue and the yaji spice hitting the flames.
s: Two decades of chilli-crusted suya over open coal
why: Consistently named Lagos's top suya destination as the city's street-food scene gains international food-media coverage.

w: A Cape Verdean-run canteen in downtown Dakar's Plateau district serving what many call the city's best yassa poulet alongside thiebou yapp and Creole classics, portions large enough for two to share off one plate. A rare Dakar institution that has outlasted decades of changing trends.
s: Cape Verdean-run canteen, Dakar's best yassa poulet
why: Remains the standing local reference for Senegalese-Creole home cooking as Dakar's dining scene draws wider attention.

w: A seafront park facing the Old Fort where, each sunset, dozens of stalls light up with skewered octopus, whole grilled lobster and the local specialty Zanzibar pizza: minced meat, egg and mayo folded into fried dough on a hot griddle. Sugarcane juice with ginger washes it all down.
s: Sunset seafood stalls facing Stone Town's Old Fort
why: Stone Town's signature nightly gathering, growing busier as Zanzibar's tourism numbers keep climbing post-pandemic.

w: Opened in 1933 on Bechara El Khoury Street by Mustapha Sahyoun and now run from Hamra by his descendants, a family feud in 2006 left two near-identical branches operating side by side, each claiming the true recipe. Both still fry the same crackling, herb-green falafel that drew Anthony Bourdain.
s: A 1933 falafel dynasty split into rival branches
why: One of the Arab world's oldest surviving falafel houses, still cited as Beirut's benchmark despite the country's economic strain.

w: A no-frills Pakistani canteen opened by Chaudary Abdul Hameed in 1978 that has barely changed since: plastic chairs, fluorescent light and cash-only counters serving butter chicken karahi, seekh kebab and daal to construction crews, cabbies and, once, a visiting Snoop Dogg.
s: Cash-only curry house that outlasted glass-tower Dubai
why: A cult fixture that has survived Dubai's transformation around it, repeatedly rediscovered by food media and celebrities.

w: A butcher counter with a handful of wooden tables wedged into the western edge of Carmel Market, opened in 2015 and now Tel Aviv's most argued-over meat address. The arayes, chargrilled lamb and tahini stuffed into pita that soaks up the meat's own juices, draws queues from opening.
s: A butcher counter behind Carmel Market's best arayes
why: Regularly ranked among the Middle East's 50 Best restaurants, credited with reviving arayes as a fine-casual dish.

w: Northern Europe's largest street-food market, built from repurposed shipping containers on a derelict shipyard island since 2018. Around thirty-five stalls and a converted machine hall serve everything from Ethiopian injera to Nordic seafood, with harbour views and a house brewery pouring alongside.
s: Shipping-container food market on a dead shipyard
why: Anchors the redevelopment of Refshaleoen into Copenhagen's edgiest food and culture district.

w: An 1892 iron-and-tile fish market that slid into decline until Time Out magazine won the concession in 2010 and curated its best chefs and stalls under one roof, opening in 2014. Half the hall still runs as a working morning market; the other half is now one of Europe's busiest food halls.
s: An 1892 fish hall reborn as a curated food hall
why: Became the template global cities copied for the curated-food-hall format, still Lisbon's single busiest dining venue.

w: A horseshoe-arched apartment block by MVRDV, opened in 2014 over ground where archaeologists found a tenth-century farmstead beneath medieval Rotterdam's first settlement. The vault's ceiling is one vast painted mural of fruit and vegetables looming over a hundred stalls of cheese and global street food.
s: A tenth-century farmstead beneath a painted food hall
why: One of Europe's most photographed food halls, its giant fresco ceiling still drawing architecture tourists a decade on.

w: Open around the clock near Tbilisi's Deserter Market since 2003, dumplings are hand-pinched to order in full view of the dining room, twisted topknot and all, then piled steaming onto tin plates. Folk music and dancing kick in after eight, but locals come mainly for the peppery meat broth inside each fold.
s: Hand-twisted khinkali, folded in view of diners
why: One of the busiest khinkali chains in Tbilisi, credited with popularising open-kitchen dumpling folding as its own spectacle.

w: The Sorbillo family opened its first pizzeria on Via dei Tribunali in 1935; grandmother Carolina raised twenty-one children who nearly all became pizzaioli. Grandson Gino took over the same address in the 1990s, and the queue for his blistered, wood-fired margherita still snakes down Naples's pizza street.
s: A pizza dynasty of twenty-one children, one street
why: Still the most queued-for stop on Naples's most concentrated pizza street, a family name synonymous with the dish itself.

w: Trading on the same site since 1803, rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1849 and expanded with pieces of an old city hall folded into its south building. Farmers still arrive at dawn on Saturdays as they have for two centuries, selling meat, cheese and produce inside a market Nat Geo once ranked the world's best.
s: Farmers selling at dawn since 1803
why: Named the world's best food market by National Geographic, a title Toronto still trades on over a decade later.

w: Founded in 1928 by Romanian immigrant Reuben Schwartz, Canada's oldest still-running deli cures its beef brisket for ten days over a brick smokehouse coated in nine decades of buildup, then hand-slices it onto rye with yellow mustard. The line down Saint-Laurent Boulevard rarely lets up.
s: Ten-day cured smoked meat, sliced since 1928
why: Canada's oldest deli still standing from before 1930, a Montreal landmark that survives generational ownership changes intact.

w: The largest open-air market in the Southern Hemisphere, built from the 1860s over Melbourne's first British cemetery, whose early settlers still lie beneath the stalls. Wednesday nights in summer and winter bring a hawker-style night market with global street food, DJs and pop-up bars under the heritage sheds.
s: Seven hectares of stalls over Melbourne's first graveyard
why: Draws around ten million visitors a year and remains the last of Melbourne's Victorian-era markets still fully operating.

w: A Saturday-morning fundraiser started in 1978 that grew into Auckland's largest Pacific market, hangi pits smoking alongside stalls of taro, chop suey and Cook Island doughnuts. Live cultural performances run through the six-till-noon window as vendors sell crafts and produce beside the food stalls.
s: Hangi smoke and Pacific crafts since 1978
why: The clearest expression of Auckland's Pasifika culture in food form, a fixture increasingly flagged in global market round-ups.
